name: Bunuba
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source.
catalog_citation: Knight, Emily Jane. 2004. Aspects of Bunuba grammar and semantics. MA (Hons) thesis, University of New England, Armidale (conferred 2005; UNE Green open access, hdl 1959.11/18646). Chapter 2 'Aspects of Bunuba grammar', sec. 2.5 Stress, pp. 24-25.
catalog_locator: Ch. 2 'Aspects of Bunuba grammar', sec. 2.5 'Stress', thesis pp. 24-25 (pp. 5-6 of the UNE chapter-2 file); endnote 2 on thesis p. 58.
catalog_quote: 2.5 Stress. The stress patterns on monomorphemic nominals and other word classes, such as mode particles, is straightforward and non-contrastive, and typical of other Australian languages. Words of between one and three syllables show primary stress on the first syllable. Words of four or five syllables show primary stress on the first syllable with secondary stress on the third syllable. Monomorphemic words of more than five syllables do not occur. 1-3 syllables: 2-7 wíyi [wiː] woman (1 syllable); bálga barramundi (2 syllables); gúmani knee (3 syllables). 4-5 syllables: 2-8 jálungùrru good (4 syllables); bályamàrada motorcar (5 syllables). When case markers or enclitics are attached to a nominal the following stress patterns arise: if the case marker/enclitic is monosyllabic it receives no stress; if the ending is two or more syllables, it receives secondary stress on its first syllable. Monosyllabic nominal endings: 2-9 rárrgi-u money-DAT; mána-way older brother-PAIR. Multi-syllabic nominal endings: 2-10 búga-yàni child-pl; míyha-bìlinyi meat-PERL; gúrama-yàni man-pl.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.citation: Knight, Emily Jane. 2004. Aspects of Bunuba grammar and semantics. MA (Hons) thesis, University of New England, Armidale. Chapter 2, sec. 2.5 Stress, pp. 24-25.
new_statements.locator: sec. 2.5 'Stress', p. 24 (first paragraph) and pp. 24-25 (enclitic paragraph); PDF pages 5-6 of the ch. 2 file
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (40 pp., OmniPage text) and extracted pp. 4-7 = thesis pp. 23-26 with extracted text; Sec. 2.5 'Stress' begins on thesis p. 24 (p. 5). The first quoted paragraph is there word for word: "The stress patterns on monomorphemic nominals and other word classes, such as mode particles, is straightforward and non-contrastive, and typical of other Australian languages. Words of between one and three syllables show primary stress on the first syllable. Words of four or five syllables show primary stress on the first syllable with secondary stress on the third syllable. Monomorphemic words of more than five syllables do not occur." The enclitic paragraph at the foot of p. 24 is also verbatim:…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is fixed on the first syllable of the word (examples wíyi 'woman', bálga 'barramundi', gúmani 'knee', jálungùrru 'good', bályamàrada 'motorcar'); it is non-contrastive. Four- and five-syllable monomorphemic words add a secondary stress on the third syllable. Monosyllabic case markers and enclitics are unstressed; a case marker or enclitic of two or more syllables carries a secondary stress on its own first syllable (búga-yàni 'child-PL', míyha-bìlinyi 'meat-PERL', gúrama-yàni 'man-PL').
new_statements.secondary_stress: On the third syllable of 4-5 syllable monomorphemic words (jálungùrru, bályamàrada); on the first syllable of any polysyllabic case marker/enclitic (búga-yàni, míyha-bìlinyi); monosyllabic endings get none.
new_statements.exceptions: Fn. 2 (p. 58) suggests the long vowel in jarraa 'far away' might reflect stress with lengthening placed on the second syllable to emphasise distance iconically; wíyi 'woman' is listed as one phonetic syllable [wi:]. Stress in verbs (coverb + auxiliary complexes) is not described in sec. 2.5, which covers nominals, mode particles and other word classes; ch. 1 notes phonological evidence that coverb and auxiliary interact as a single word (sec. 3.3, chapter 3 file not among the open files).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level: monomorphemic nominals, mode particles and 'other word classes', and nominal plus case marker/enclitic; described impressionistically from fieldwork with ten Junjuwa (Fitzroy Crossing) speakers of both the light and heavy dialects; no instrumental data.
new_statements.identity_note: Knight 2004 describes contemporary Bunuba as spoken at Junjuwa (Fitzroy Crossing), with consultants from both the 'light' (western) and 'heavy' dialects (sec. 1.3.1, Table 1-3); the stress rule is given for the language as a whole with no dialect split. Same variety as Glottolog buna1275 (ISO bck).

new_statements.quote: 2.3 STRESS Monomorphemic words of one, two, or three syllables have primary stress on the first syllable. Those with four or five syllables have primary stress on the first syllable and secondary on the third. Examples of stress-marked two-to-four syllable words can be found among the forms cited in §2.1 above. A five-syllable example is: miljidawurru 'storm from the south' [...] Words with vowel-reduced /ir/ sequences (as discussed in 2.1) are treated as if the rule for stress placement follows that of vowel reduction, as evident from the examples given there. Polymorphemic words show other, more complicated stress patterns which are best discussed as the morphology is introduced.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement and type as the catalog record (Knight 2004: initial primary stress, secondary on the third syllable in 4-5-syllable words, non-contrastive) -- Knight's sec. 2.5 closely follows Rumsey's sec. 2.3. Rumsey 2000 is the primary reference grammar and adds the r-colouring/vowel-reduction exception, the reduplication stress facts and the aberrant finally-stressed interjection ag'a. No contradiction.
new_statements.rule_in_words: In monomorphemic words primary stress falls on the first syllable; words of four or five syllables add a secondary stress on the third syllable (alternating rhythm). Syllables with vowel-reduced /ir/ (i merging into a following r after g/b) do not count for stress placement / tend to lose primary stress. Polymorphemic words (reduplications, preverb'auxiliary verb complexes) have more complex patterns treated in the morphology: e.g. partial reduplications shift primary stress onto the base (ma'mabilyi), full reduplication keeps initial primary stress ('mamumamu); the interjection ag'a is explicitly flagged as aberrant for being stressed on its last syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on the third syllable of four- and five-syllable monomorphemic words (e.g. miljidawurru 'storm from the south', jalungurru [·òaluªNøru] with secondary mark on the third syllable).
new_statements.exceptions: (i) r-coloured vowels: 'syllables which would otherwise have primary stress tend to lose it' before /r/, and words with reduced /ir/ (giriywa 'wind', biriyali, biray) place stress as if the reduced syllable were absent; (ii) polymorphemic words have 'other, more complicated stress patterns'; reduplication types [a]-[d] carry primary stress after the reduplicant (ga'ndaynday, ngarra'ngarranyi) while type [e] full reduplication retains initial primary stress; (iii) interjection ag'a 'not so' is stressed on the last syllable, noted as phonologically aberrant ('no other independent words.. are stressed on the last syllable if they have more than one').
new_statements.identity_note: Bunuba (formerly spelled Bunaba, Punaba, Buniba, Bunapa), non-Pama-Nyungan, Bunaban family, spoken in and around Fitzroy Crossing, Kimberley, Western Australia; Rumsey's sketch is based on his own fieldwork and notes no dialect split relevant to stress.

sources.note: First-hand: stress is non-contrastive; words of 1-3 syllables have primary stress on the first syllable; words of 4-5 syllables have primary stress on the first and secondary on the third syllable; monomorphemic words of more than five syllables do not occur; a monosyllabic case marker/enclitic is unstressed, a 2+ syllable ending takes secondary stress on its first syllable (buga-yani, miyha-bilinyi, gurama-yani). Fn. 2 (p. 58): long vowel of jarraa 'far away' possibly stress shifted to 2nd syllable for iconic emphasis.
